content: 1. Pretomanid and OAT3 Substrates: In vitro studies indicate that pretomanid significantly inhibits the organic anion transporter 3 (OAT3). This may lead to increased adverse effects when co-administered with OAT3 substrates. Close monitoring is recommended, and dosage adjustments for OAT3 substrates should be considered. 2. Calcium Carbonate and Propranolol: Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of propranolol by decreasing its gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. To minimize this effect, administer calcium carbonate at least 2 hours apart from propranolol. 3. Calcium Carbonate and Quinapril: Calcium carbonate decreases the effects of quinapril through an unspecified mechanism. Close monitoring is advised when these agents are used together. 4. Calcium Carbonate and Quinidine: Calcium carbonate increases quinidine levels by enhancing passive renal tubular reabsorption in a basic urine environment. Elevated quinidine plasma levels may result in cardiac conduction disturbances or arrhythmias. Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Magnesium Hydroxide and Raltegravir: Magnesium hydroxide reduces raltegravir levels by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract. This interaction can significantly lower raltegravir plasma concentrations if taken within 6 hours of each other. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 6. Calcium Carbonate and Ramipril: Calcium carbonate decreases the effects of ramipril through an unspecified mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Calcium Carbonate and Rifampin: Calcium carbonate reduces rifampin absorption when taken together. Rifampin should be administered at least 1 hour before antacids to avoid this interaction. 8. Famotidine and Rilpivirine: Famotidine decreases rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially leading to treatment failure or resistance. Antacids should be administered at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. For combination products like dolutegravir/rilpivirine, antacids should be given at least 4 hours before or 6 hours after. 9. Magnesium Hydroxide and Riociguat: Magnesium hydroxide reduces riociguat levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Administer these agents at least 1 hour apart. 10. Calcium Carbonate and Risedronate: Calcium carbonate decreases risedronate levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Administer risedronate at least 2 hours apart from calcium carbonate. 11. Famotidine and Risedronate: Famotidine increases risedronate levels by altering gastric pH, which may accelerate the dissolution of delayed-release formulations. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 12. Calcium Carbonate and Rosuvastatin: Calcium carbonate reduces rosuvastatin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Administer these agents at least 2 hours apart. 13. Calcium Carbonate and Salicylates: Calcium carbonate alters salicylate levels depending on the dose. Moderate doses increase salicylate levels, while large doses decrease them due to increased renal excretion of unchanged salicylic acid. 14. Magnesium Hydroxide and Sarecycline: Magnesium hydroxide reduces sarecycline levels by impairing gastrointestinal absorption. Separate dosing of sarecycline and magnesium hydroxide to avoid reduced efficacy. 15. Famotidine and Secretin: Famotidine may cause a hyperresponse in gastrin secretion during secretin stimulation testing, falsely suggesting gastrinoma. Discontinue H2-receptor antagonists at least 2 days before secretin administration. 16. Famotidine and Serdexmethylphenidate/Dexmethylphenidate: Famotidine increases the levels of these medications by altering gastric pH. This interaction applies only to extended-release formulations. 17. Calcium Carbonate and Sodium Phosphates: Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of sodium phosphates by binding dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract. Use alternatives if available. 18. Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate and Calcium Carbonate: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate increases calcium carbonate levels by reducing renal clearance, potentially leading to alkalosis. 19. Magnesium Sulfate/Potassium Chloride and Calcium Carbonate: Co-administration with medications causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Monitor closely. 20. Calcium Carbonate and Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir: Calcium carbonate reduces velpatasvir solubility by increasing gastric pH, potentially decreasing efficacy. Administer H2-receptor antagonists 12 hours apart or simultaneously with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir at doses not exceeding famotidine 40 mg BID. 21. Calcium Carbonate and Sotalol: Calcium carbonate reduces sotalol levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Administer these agents at least 2 hours apart. 22. Magnesium Hydroxide and Tetracyclines: Magnesium hydroxide impairs tetracycline absorption, reducing efficacy. Separate dosing to avoid this interaction. 23. Famotidine and Vandetanib: Co-administration may increase QTc interval prolongation, leading to potential toxicity. Avoid or use alternative drugs. 24. Vitamin D and Calcium Carbonate: Vitamin D increases calcium carbonate levels through pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely, especially in patients with renal impairment. 25. Calcium Carbonate and Zoledronic Acid: Calcium carbonate reduces zoledronic acid levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Administer zoledronic acid at least 30 minutes apart from calcium carbonate. 26. General Warnings for H2-Receptor Antagonists: Use caution in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, as dosage adjustments may be necessary. Prolonged QT intervals and torsades de pointes have been reported in patients with renal impairment. Relief of symptoms does not rule out gastric malignancy. Pediatric patients may have an increased risk of acute gastroenteritis and community-acquired pneumonia. Some formulations may contain benzyl alcohol or sodium benzoate, which are associated with gasping syndrome in neonates. 27. Pregnancy Safety: H2-receptor antagonists are generally considered safe during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
